title: Knowledge Check 2 - Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 - Data Modeling/Database Design. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: An architect needs to know which users changed a validation rule last quarter. Which native tool answers this?
options: Field History Tracking
The Setup Audit Trail
The Metadata API
Data Loader
questions.explanation: The Setup Audit Trail records configuration changes by user/date; field history (A) tracks record data, the Metadata API (C) is for retrieval/deploy, and Data Loader (D) moves records.

questions.question: Which TWO tools give machine-readable metadata suitable for change control and cataloging?
options: The Metadata API
A page layout
The Tooling API
A standard report
questions.explanation: The Metadata API (A) and Tooling API (C) expose metadata programmatically; layouts and reports are not metadata-management substrates.

questions.question: A governance program requires that every new field carry a description and owner. Which approach makes this a repeatable control rather than a one-time task?
options: Manual review in each release
An automated conformance report/check over the org's metadata
Requiring developers to remember the rule
Encrypting fields by default
questions.explanation: Automated conformance monitoring turns the standard into an ongoing control; manual/remembered checks and encryption do not enforce metadata completeness.

questions.question: A customer must retain 8 years of audit events (billions of rows) on the platform for compliance, with occasional aggregate extracts. Which store is most appropriate?
options: A standard custom object
A Big Object with an index and Async SOQL extracts
External Objects via Salesforce Connect
A skinny table
questions.explanation: Big Objects are built for this scale and retention, with Async SOQL for extracts; a standard object would hit limits (A), External Objects virtualize rather than store (C), and skinny tables are a query-optimization aid, not massive storage (D).

questions.question: Which TWO capabilities do Big Objects NOT provide?
options: Composite primary key and index definition
Standard roll-up summary fields and triggers
Standard interactive reporting and page layouts
Bulk ingestion
questions.explanation: Big Objects omit roll-ups/triggers (B) and standard reporting/layouts (C); the composite key/index (A) and Bulk ingestion (D) are supported.

questions.question: What is the primary role of Async SOQL with Big Objects?
options: To synchronously render Big Object records in the UI
To run an asynchronous query/aggregation and write results to a target
To create indexes automatically
To enforce validation rules on Big Object writes
questions.explanation: Async SOQL runs as a background job and writes results to a target object/file; it does not provide synchronous UI (A), auto-indexing (C), or validation (D).

questions.question: A service org's Case object has 200M rows and slow list views; 95% of cases are closed and only referenced for compliance lookups. What is the best design?
options: Increase the Case object's index and keep all rows
Archive closed cases older than the retention threshold to a Big Object and delete them from Case
Move all cases to a Big Object immediately
Enable Salesforce Connect over Case
questions.explanation: Archiving old closed cases wins back LDV performance while retaining compliance data; raising limits (A) does not solve scale, moving all cases (C) breaks interactive use, and Connect (D) virtualizes rather than resolves volume.

questions.question: Which TWO scenarios argue AGAINST using a Big Object?
options: Users must interactively edit records and run standard reports
Billions of immutable event records must be retained for years
The data must participate in roll-up summary fields and validation rules
Bulk ingestion of high-volume telemetry
questions.explanation: Interactive editing/reporting (A) and roll-up/validation participation (C) are not supported by Big Objects; retention of immutable events (B) and bulk ingestion (D) are exactly Big Object strengths.

questions.question: A customer needs a single view that blends recent interactive records with 10 years of history, without duplicating history onto the platform. Which approach fits?
options: Store all history in a Big Object only
Keep recent data in a standard object and virtualize old data via an External Object
Copy all history into a custom object
Disable Big Objects and use only External Objects
questions.explanation: A hybrid - recent native plus virtualized external history - avoids duplication and supports a unified view; Big-Object-only (A) loses interactivity, copying all history (C) defeats virtualizing, and external-only (D) removes native recent data.

questions.question: Contacts bulk-load fails with row-lock timeouts because millions of contacts all point to one Account. What is the most direct mitigation?
options: Increase the batch size and parallelize harder
Shard the account relationship so children distribute across multiple parents
Change the lookup to a master-detail relationship
Set the Account OWD to public
questions.explanation: This is lookup skew on a hot parent; distributing children across intermediate parents relieves the parent lock, whereas parallelizing harder (A) increases contention, MD (C) worsens locking, and OWD (D) is unrelated.

questions.question: Which TWO factors contribute to data skew problems?
options: A single owner/queue holding a very large share of records
A large number of child records all referencing one parent record
A private organization-wide default
A shallow role hierarchy
questions.explanation: Ownership skew (A) and lookup skew (B) are the two named skew types; private OWD (C) and a shallow hierarchy (D) do not cause skew.

questions.question: An architect is told that deferring sharing calculation during a bulk load is required. Why?
options: It encrypts the data during load
It avoids re-running sharing recalculation for every batched insert, which is expensive under skew
It bypasses duplicate rules
It enables Big Object ingestion
questions.explanation: Deferring sharing defers the expensive recalculation until after the load; it does not encrypt (A), bypass duplicates (C), or relate to Big Objects (D).

questions.question: A design has one Account with 5M related Notes, and any update to that Account locks. Which pattern BEST removes the concentration?
options: Add a roll-up summary to the Account
Introduce intermediate parent records (shards) so Notes distribute across many parents
Convert Note lookups to master-detail
Enable Big Objects and keep the relationship
questions.explanation: Sharding across intermediate parents removes the single hot parent; roll-ups (A) and MD (C) worsen locking, and Big Objects (D) cannot participate in the relationship.

questions.question: Which TWO design patterns help avoid data skew?
options: Polymorphic relationships that fan references across multiple parents
A single queue owning all integration-loaded records
Junction objects that distribute many-to-many relationships
A roll-up summary on the most heavily referenced parent
questions.explanation: Polymorphic lookups (A) and junction objects (C) distribute references; a single owning queue (B) creates ownership skew and heavily-referenced roll-ups (D) worsen lock contention.

questions.question: Why is denormalization sometimes a skew mitigation rather than a cost?
options: It encrypts records to avoid locks
It removes the need for a hot parent lookup on frequent paths by carrying the value on the child
It moves records to a Big Object
It increases the fan-out to the parent
questions.explanation: Denormalizing the value onto children removes hot-path parent access and its locking; it does not encrypt (A), archive (C), or increase fan-out (D).
